title: When the Algorithm Reads the Scan
body:
Deep-learning systems now identify abnormalities in medical images with an accuracy that rivals, and in several tasks exceeds, that of junior clinicians. Yet comparatively few have reached routine hospital use. The gap between reported performance and deployed performance is not mysterious: it follows from how such systems are validated, and from the fact that a model which performs well in an experiment is not automatically a device which performs well at the bedside. Grounding a claim in a single retrospective test has become a habit that the clinical setting cannot reward. Commercial interest is considerable, and the pressure to publish a flattering number is real.

Most published evaluations are retrospective. Records from existing hospital systems are annotated by experts, a model is trained and tested on the same collection, and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve looks impressive. What such a design cannot show is how the system will behave on patients who arrive next week, in a different building, with scanners from another manufacturer. Because the same patient population and the same machines appear on both sides of the split, the result measures how well the system fits a particular cohort, not how robust it is.

The central technical question is generalisation, and its failure mode has a name: drift. Once a model is deployed in one centre, it decays slowly as referral patterns shift, as imaging protocols are revised, and as new equipment replaces the scanners on which it was trained. Reported accuracy may be quoted once and never revisited; unless a mechanism observes the live inputs, the decline is discovered only after a clinician notices that the character of a report has changed. Prospective validation, in which a system runs alongside normal care for a defined period and every disagreement is logged, costs more and is usually skipped. The institutions that own such a system rarely hold the instrumentation needed to detect it.

Bias introduces a second, quieter problem. Training collections over-represent some groups and under-represent others, generally because access to advanced imaging has never been equal. A model fitted to that mixture inherits the imbalance and may produce markedly different false positive rates across populations, presenting a screening tool that is unusually cautious, or unusually indiscriminate, for particular groups of patients. Aggregate benchmarks conceal the problem: an average conceals the tail, and a headline figure rarely travels down to the subgroup that is worst served.

Integration is a practical problem as much as a clinical one. A system that returns a verdict in seconds is of little use if it cannot be embedded in the workflow a radiologist already follows, if its output arrives in a format that the picture archiving system will not display, or if it interrupts the sequence of decisions through which a scan is normally read. Latency, interface and the established habits of the reading room together determine whether a genuinely useful model is ever used, and none of them appears in an accuracy table. A model that cannot be embedded is, in practice, a model that will be switched off within a year.

Reproducibility is uneven across the field. Papers frequently omit the annotation protocol, the exact exclusion rules or the version of the code that produced the numbers, so an independent group cannot reconstruct the experiment even when the underlying data can be requested. Provenance, which images, which labels, which adjudication, by whom, is what turns a result into evidence. Where such records are kept, the checks are cheap and fast; where they are absent, a published figure can be reproduced only by the authors who produced it, and the field loses the ability to learn from its own experiments.

Regulators have responded by treating these systems as medical devices subject to audit rather than as ordinary software releases. Approval requires a documented validation strategy, a defined intended use, and post-market surveillance that monitors drift and adverse events. Several frameworks now insist on a human in the loop: an algorithm may flag, rank or prioritise images, but a qualified reader must remain accountable for the report. The rule is easy to state and expensive to satisfy, since it obliges each hospital to record who saw what, and when.

The question that remains open is accountability. When a model returns a false negative and a patient is harmed, no honest account can say that the machine decided. Somebody trained the system, chose its intended use, procured the software and signed the report. Distributing responsibility across those actors is difficult, but the difficulty is not technical: it is a matter of allocating duty among developers, hospitals and clinicians. Until that allocation is written down, a sophisticated algorithm will continue to reach clinics faster than the accountability that ought to arrive with it. Regulators, insurers and hospitals each prefer the others to define the standard.
